source.title: Erase Persona, Forget Lore: Benchmarking Multimodal Copyright Unlearning in Large Vision Language Models
source.authors: Junehyoung Kwon; Jung-Ki Yun; Youngbin Kim

record.tranche_reason: Applies several unlearning methods to LVLMs and measures forgetting and retained utility, but does not test recovery attacks or reproduce a specific recovery-attack protocol.
record.gate_note: The study tests unlearning efficacy and utility, not recovery through fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization, or prompting. Table 1 reports stage-1 memorization before unlearning; it is not a recovery-attack result and is not included as a row. Figures 2–4 report additional aggregate trends; their values are shown only in figures, so the numeric Table 2 results are recorded instead.
record.test_reason: The study applies five standard unlearning methods (GA, GD, KL, DPO, NPO) to two LVLMs on a new synthetic-copyright benchmark. It reports forget-set and held-out forgetting alongside retained utility, which bears directly on whether unlearning reaches strong forgetting while keeping ability (A). Its modality-gap analysis shows knowledge forgotten under text queries remaining reachable through image queries, which bears on E. It runs no fine-tuning, internal-edit, quantization or robust-method tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that current methods either erase effectively by collapsing utility or keep utility while failing to erase. They also report a modality gap: methods struggle to sever the vision–knowledge link even when textual associations are removed.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates standard gradient-based and preference-based unlearning in LVLMs using a synthetic copyright benchmark; does not implement the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model size, unlearning method, query modality, forget ratio, and copyright domain, as described in Figures 2–4; figure values are not transcribed here.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors read high Divergence with low Efficacy for DPO, NPO and GD as a learned superficial refusal rather than forgetting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Preference-based unlearning in LVLMs yields refusal-style outputs without erasing keyword knowledge (an output-level, not internal, analysis).

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation
record.problems: Only two LVLMs and synthetic copyright concepts are tested. The study reports no uncertainty estimates and no chance-level reference for the forgetting metrics. It does not test any recovery attack. The modality-gap and forget-ratio analyses are presented as figures without numeric values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: None from Table 2; its 60 model × method × metric results are recorded. Figure 2–4 aggregate results are not separately extracted because the supplied text gives no numeric values for them.

untested.parts: Whether fine-tuning, internal-edit or quantization attacks recover the forgotten knowledge; chance-level reference for the keyword metrics.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
All: no activation ablation or internal analysis. The refusal interpretation rests only on output divergence.
Jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information. Only the shift from text to image queries, and held-out compositions, are probed.
All: no method is claimed or tested as robust to attacks.

missing.what: Single-modal vs multi-modal Efficacy/Specificity per method (modality gap); GA/KL forget text associations but not image-linked ones
Forget ratio 5%→20%: GA/KL/NPO reach perfect erasure with fluency and specificity at 0; GD/DPO efficacy below 10
Domain split: KL efficacy 92.5 on logos vs 87.4 on characters; NPO 24.92-point higher efficacy on characters

record.verdict_notes: New setting (LVLMs, synthetic copyright concepts), so this is T3, not T2. The reader's single blanket limits_scope label is split by condition group. Fluency and specificity rows can use Table 1 stage-1 ROUGE and EM as approximate baselines; Table 1 is measured on Dtrain rather than Dretain′, so these baselines are approximate. Divergence rows stay cannot_determine because refusals inflate dissimilarity. The E verdict rests on prose about a figure with no numbers. No uncertainty is reported, and only two models are tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures keyword-based forgetting and retained capability/utility after unlearning. It does not test whether attacks recover knowledge, and it does not report a chance-level reference for the targeted-knowledge metrics.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or other relearning attack.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis testing whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language-switching, or in-context recovery attack.
No method is tested for resistance to the recovery attacks listed in the claim.

relation.reason: Its own forgetting and utility results bear on version A.

tranche.reason: A new setting (copyright unlearning in LVLMs) where standard methods give results on forgetting and retained utility, bearing on A. There are no recovery attacks, so not T1. It is a benchmark, not aimed at the original's question, so T3 rather than T2.

source_check.notes: Table 1 Stage-1 values: 3B ROUGE 76.63, EM Dtrain 99.65, Acc 74.86; 7B ROUGE 78.15, EM Dtrain 99.94, Acc 73.55, so the 7B capability baseline is 73.55, not 74.86. Single runs, LoRA r=64 in both stages, no recovery attacks. Figures 2-4 give no numbers in the text and name no model. Figure 4's KL Efficacy 92.5/87.4 does not match Table 2 (72.09 on 7B), so its setting is unclear.

statements.correction: LLaVA-1.5-7B GD, 5% forget ratio: Efficacy 7.50, Generality 10.69 (Table 2), i.e. 92.5% keyword recall kept on Dforget; Stage-1 EM(Dtrain) 99.94 (Table 1); LoRA r=64, alpha=128 in both stages; single runs, no error bars, no chance level.
statements.problem: Nothing wrong about this study. The pre-unlearning 'about 0' is derived from Stage-1 EM(Dtrain) 99.94, not tabulated as Efficacy. Small omissions: EM here is keyword recall, and this study also uses LoRA.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All five methods on LLaVA-Phi-3B and LLaVA-1.5-7B at 5% forget ratio
reader_labels.reason: Table 2 shows a trade-off: GA/KL have stronger keyword forgetting but incur utility costs on the 7B model, while GD/DPO/NPO preserve utility to varying degrees but the authors say they fail at true erasure; see r01–r60. Recovery attacks and chance-level performance were not tested.
